recall.define: Define heap corruption, double free, stack exhaustion, off-by-one error, allocation failure and asynchronous lifetime without the glossary and name the source behind each.
recall.distinguish: Give the distinction and a four-line C example for: use-after-free versus double free; stack exhaustion versus stack corruption; out-of-bounds access versus off-by-one error; memory leak versus retention; indeterminate representation versus heap corruption.
recall.apply: A ring buffer of records is resized with realloc while a DMA transfer still targets the old block. Name every term that applies (resize invalidation, asynchronous lifetime, use-after-free, heap corruption), say which tool observation (AddressSanitizer report, Valgrind memcheck, fixed-region collision at startup) would reveal it first, and which repair restores the ownership invariant.

entries.definition: Damage to the allocator's own bookkeeping (chunk headers, free lists) or to a neighboring allocation caused by an out-of-bounds write, a double free or an invalid free; the symptom usually appears later, inside malloc or free, far from the cause.
idiom: the abort inside free is the symptom of earlier heap corruption
entries.misconception: A crash in malloc means the allocator is broken.

entries.definition: Passing the same pointer to free twice without an intervening allocation of the same address; the behavior is undefined, and allocators may silently corrupt their free lists or abort. The curriculum also calls the generic case a double release when the resource is not heap memory.
entries.misconception: free(p); free(p); is harmless if nothing was allocated in between.

entries.definition: Calling free on a pointer that did not come from malloc, calloc, realloc or aligned_alloc, such as an interior pointer, a stack address or a pointer from another allocator; undefined behavior that typically corrupts the heap.
entries.misconception: Freeing a pointer to the middle of a block frees the tail.

entries.definition: Running out of stack space through deep recursion, large automatic arrays or a too-small configured stack; on Linux it ends in SIGSEGV on the guard page, on a Cortex-M it overruns into whatever lies below the stack unless an MPU guard or stack limit register catches it.

distinguish_from.distinction: Exhaustion is running past the end of the stack; corruption is an out-of-bounds write inside a frame that damages saved registers or the return address.

entries.misconception: Stack overflow always produces an immediate fault.

entries.definition: Overwriting data in a stack frame (saved return address, saved registers, neighboring locals) through an out-of-bounds write into an automatic array; the stack protector detects the sequential case, the symptom is often a return to a wrong address.
entries.misconception: Stack corruption and stack exhaustion are the same failure.

entries.definition: A bound computed one element too far or too short, typically from confusing a count with the last valid index or forgetting the terminating null character; the most common source of a one-byte out-of-bounds write.
entries.misconception: A one-byte overrun past an array is too small to matter.

entries.definition: A buffer treated as a string although no null character lies within its bounds, often after strncpy filled it completely or a length-limited read stopped early; every subsequent str* call reads out of bounds.
The invalidation of every pointer into a block when realloc moves it; the old pointers become dangling even though the bytes were copied, and the old block must not be freed or used.
entries.misconception: realloc grows the block in place.

entries.definition: A null pointer returned by malloc, calloc or realloc because the request cannot be satisfied; code that assumes success dereferences a null pointer, and code that writes p = realloc(p, n) loses the original block on failure.
entries.misconception: malloc never fails on Linux (overcommit only delays the failure to the first touch).

entries.definition: Storage that is still reachable and still allocated but no longer needed, such as a cache that never evicts; unlike a memory leak it can be released, yet it exhausts memory just the same.
entries.misconception: A leak checker that reports nothing means memory use is bounded.

entries.definition: Overlap between statically placed regions of a firmware image (stack, heap, .data, .bss, retained sections) caused by a linker-script or startup error, so that one region's growth silently overwrites another; detected by linker assertions, map-file inspection and fill-pattern checks, not by tests alone.
entries.misconception: A successful link proves the memory layout is consistent.

entries.definition: An object whose lifetime must outlast the function that created it because a DMA controller, a completion callback or another thread still refers to it; freeing or reusing it before the asynchronous consumer finishes is a use-after-free that no single-threaded test shows.
entries.misconception: The buffer can be freed once the submit call returns.

entries.definition: Compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=address) that surrounds allocations with redzones and tracks freed memory in quarantine so that out-of-bounds accesses, use-after-free, double free and some stack errors abort with a diagnosed stack trace; it observes only executed paths and roughly doubles memory and time.

authority.locator: 5.2 Continuing and Stepping — continue, step, next, finish, until, stepi and nexti

entries.misconception: AddressSanitizer finds all memory errors (uninitialized reads need MemorySanitizer or Valgrind, and unexecuted paths are never checked).

entries.definition: Valgrind's default tool, which runs an uninstrumented binary under dynamic translation and tracks definedness bit by bit, reporting uninitialized reads, invalid accesses, invalid frees and leaks at a large slowdown; complementary to AddressSanitizer rather than redundant with it.

authority.locator: 5.2 Continuing and Stepping — continue, step, next, finish, until, stepi and nexti

entries.misconception: Valgrind and AddressSanitizer report the same defects.

entries.definition: A handle that pairs a slot index with a generation counter incremented on every release of the slot, so that a stale handle to a reused slot is rejected instead of aliasing the new occupant; the curriculum's standard defense against stale-identity reuse in pools.
entries.misconception: Reusing a freed slot index is safe once the slot is reinitialized.

entries.definition: Deliberately making an allocation, I/O or backend operation fail at a scheduled point to exercise the error path; a memory-failure drill injects allocation failure and truncation and checks that invariants, cleanup and reporting survive.
entries.misconception: Error paths that are never executed are correct because they are simple.
